blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Some issues, Mr Myers?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, yes. One matter we've brought to the prosecution's attention and the attention of your Lordship was a LinkedIn post over the weekend, venturing opinions from someone in a professional/semi-professional capacity on this case, those opinions then exciting responses in the way that happens on LinkedIn with a succession of comments that followed that. I won't repeat the content of it here, but of course the prosecution have been provided with it, as has your Lordship.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We're grateful for the steps taken by the prosecution. Mr Johnson will be better able to inform your Lordship as to that, but I should say for our part, recognising that these posts can happen and may happen yet, my instructing solicitor will be writing to the Attorney General and requesting him to consider this in the context of contempt of court and whether any action follows. Plainly, we would submit -- we would submit it plainly crosses the line. That's as far as we can take that now, but we will be notifying the Attorney General.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, we deliberately resist drawing any judgements as to whether or not things cross the line, but we recognise the problem and we recognise the potential for further problems. What the police have done is to contact LinkedIn, inviting them to remove the material and also contacted the individual concerned, in effect putting her on notice that what she is doing might be viewed as being a contempt of court and inviting her not to repeat and to remove the material.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We believe that this isn't an isolated incident in the sense of others are expressing views online, which they'd be better not expressing, and when they come to our notice, we'll do what we can. But the police can't police the internet. We have done what we can.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Thank you both very much. I think that the positions that both sides are taking are entirely appropriate.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is an inevitability of the modern technological era and, human nature being what human nature is, these things happen. But I am going to say and do nothing more at this stage and just leave things as have been indicated.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We understand, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Then we are now otherwise in a position to proceed?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Jury in, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)

Good morning, members of the jury. I'm sorry it's a little bit late. I in fact was ready to proceed at 11 o'clock, but there have been some other issues, including technology issues, but we are now in a position to proceed. So obviously we'll just go straight through to lunch.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, the Crown propose to proceed now to the cases of [Baby A] and [Baby B], counts 1 and 2 on the indictment.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Before we do that and following on from Friday's introduction, we have plans of the neonatal unit to complement the video that the jury saw. We were proposing to circulate those now, if we may.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We do so with two apologies in advance.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Firstly, the hole punching. Two of the holes are correct, two aren't, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Secondly, already the index on the front of the jury bundle is effectively obsolete, so I'm going to ask if the ladies and gentlemen of the jury wouldn't mind taking out their indices, please, perhaps passing them to the table at the end and we'll replace them as soon as we can.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
If everyone has the plan, if it assists, the video that we saw on Friday, if we look to the bottom of the plan, the larger picture on the right, which concentrates on the neonatal unit --
I think one of the problems, it's been hole punched as portrait and you have to look at it landscape.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm holding it like that, sorry (indicating).
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I haven't put it in my file yet because I find it easier to do it this way.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the right of your document you will see the whole of the ground floor of the hospital, that wing of the hospital, to put into perspective the location of the neonatal unit, which is shaded in green in the top left-hand corner as we look.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the left is a scaled-in model, if I can put it that way, of the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Within the green shading are the rooms, the nurseries that you're going to hear about in evidence, and if it assists, at the bottom of that green-shaded area you can see a door with a lock, the symbol of a lock. That's where the video entered, that lowest-most door. You may recall the cameraman or woman
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: proceeding along the corridor with the various utility rooms, if I can put them that way, on their left.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If you imagine that walk now, you would then see ahead of you at the end of that corridor nursery 1, which you have heard is the intensive care nursery.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If you were to turn left at the door of nursery 1 and continue on there, you'd see immediately on your right the nurses' station. You can probably all imagine the type of location and work that goes on there. Along that corridor in front of the nurses' station, if I can put it that way, are nurseries 2, 3 and 4 next to each other.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just, again, I hope, for your assistance, where it says "neonatal unit", immediately to the right is another locked door, and you'll see that that door leads between the neonatal unit and on one side the theatre and, on the other side, the delivery room. So you can see how close the neonatal unit is placed to the locations where the babies were born. You might hear something about that in a moment.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And as identified on the plan, this is how the rooms were being used at the time?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At the time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because, of course, the difficulty with the walk-through was that the commentator was repeatedly saying, "This was such-and-such a room at the time" --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's why we thought it might help to have it now.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I think it is helpful -- I'm used to seeing these things and it's quite difficult when they go in and they spin around, you lose track as to where they're actually looking with the camera and it's not easy to follow the geography. It may be, I don't know, if at some time it might be appropriate to play some of that again, just the walk-through bit.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: With the plan?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: With the plan. As I said, if you want anything to be replayed at any stage, please just ask.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Anything that is adduced in evidence and becomes evidence in the case, an exhibit, a recording, documents like that, are all there in evidence and available for you. Obviously it's a video that has to be played or a recording that has to be played, then it has to be played again, but you can, obviously, using your
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: iPads, look at documents as such. But the walk-through you'd have to see again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm helpfully reminded that on the iPad presentations that we have, I'm sure everyone will remember this, on the left hand button to the top of the screen is an objects list. If that's selected, one can scroll down to the video, but we're more than happy to play it again in evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The difficulty with that is the iPads have to be in court and it can be done that way. Let's leave it for the moment, but it's just there if needed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm going to begin by reading some statements for this part of the case.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Would my Lord like me to explain?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'll explain because it follows on and is linked to the agreed facts. Do you remember on Friday of last week, I told you about agreed facts, the way in which what is agreed evidence can be put before you?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The advantage of agreed facts is it's all in writing and you've got it there for you to refer to at any stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Another way in which agreed evidence can be given is, rather than a witness who gives evidence and comes to court and is asked questions and gives their evidence in this way, the witness statement made by the witness can be read to you as evidence in the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is evidence in the case, obviously for you to consider, but it's agreed evidence. In other words, it's evidence that the defence don't challenge and don't dispute, so the facts of which a witness speaks are agreed facts essentially. That's the same thing. So it's agreed evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As I said to you with agreed facts, the significance of any evidence is for you to decide, the use to which you put it is for you to decide, but you don't have to judge the reliability of the witness or the truthfulness of the witness. That's all agreed. The significance of it, how it affects your decisionmaking process at the end of the day, entirely for you, all right? But you don't get copies of the witness statements. So listen carefully.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As you will probably know, at the end of the case, after all the evidence has been called, I will give you written directions of law, counsel will address you in relation to the evidence on the issues and I will remind you of the evidence on the salient issues in the case, but I obviously can't remind you of everything that's been said, that would take almost as long as the trial had taken up to that point. But you have a lot of evidence on your iPads, you'll be making notes, some of you, of certain facts that you consider important. But I'm just saying this: don't be too worried about retaining everything, you can't possibly retain everything. A lot of the evidence is not controversial.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You will, as I said at the very outset, soon know where the controversial areas are and what the evidence is on those controversial issues. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of [Mother of Babies A & B] (read)
Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The first statement I am going to read -- I think my Lord has a bundle of these for case management purposes --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I do, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- is that of [Mother of Babies A & B]. And her witness statement was provided on 24 November 2017.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, perhaps at this stage if I read the declaration just once and then everybody then knows this is effectively at the start of, I think, a number of statements read. This is at the start of every statement and you can assume that to be the case if I just read it the once now.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly. What's going to happen is -- some of you may have made a witness statement to the police, I don't know. I have, but then I'm quite old.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But this is the statutory declaration that everyone makes when they make a witness statement basically saying that what I'm saying is the truth and I know if I'm lying I'm liable to be prosecuted for not telling the truth.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You'll hear the actual words now.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "This statement, each signed by me, is true to the best of my knowledge and belief and I make it knowing that if it is tendered in evidence I shall be liable to prosecution if I have wilfully stated in it anything wish I know to be false or do not believe to be true."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a declaration that is signed by each witness from whom you will hear statements read during the course of this trial and I think I've already mentioned that is signed on 24 November 2017.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The statement reads as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am [Mother of Babies A & B]. My fiancé is known to everybody as [Father of Babies A & B]. In February 2011 I was diagnosed with a rare blood disorder called antiphospholipid syndrome."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I will refer to that as APS from now on if I may.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is described in the statement as:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A blood-clotting disorder which causes my blood to thicken and therefore makes me prone to blood clots."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can pause there please and turn to divider 2 in your bundles and the glossary which you are all now familiar with. At the foot of page 1, the very first page on that particular document, you'll find a more detailed explanation of APS:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A disorder of the immune system that causes an increased risk of blood clots. People with APS are at greater risk of developing conditions such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a blood clot that usually develops in the leg."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So there's a slightly more detailed explanation insofar as it's relevant in this case:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "To counteract this, I was prescribed with warfarin to help thin my blood and I have been under one of the lead specialists in this field, a Professor Hannah Cohen, from the University College of London. I have annual appointments with her in London. When I was initially diagnosed, Professor Cohen and I discussed the complications of pregnancy. It was suggested that when I was ready to have a family, I would change my medication from warfarin to heparin injections with a daily dose of aspirin and this had been planned in advance of any pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Following an extended four-month holiday visiting family in Australia during the winter of 2014, [Father of Babies A & B] and I returned home to the UK to discover that I had fallen pregnant. It was on 13 December 2014. I know this because it was the day before [Father of Babies A & B]'s 30th birthday.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: This wasn't a planned pregnancy and our initial thoughts were around my diagnosis of APS. We visited my GP first and I was
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: immediately switched over to heparin injections from warfarin as heparin is safer during pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As I was already under the specialist, Professor Cohen in London, an appointment was made for [Father of Babies A & B] and I to travel down the following week to discuss my pregnancy. We discussed at length with Professor Cohen how to manage my pregnancy and the decision was made that Professor Cohen would manage my blood condition, working with my GP here locally.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The agreed plan was for me to remain at home up to 30 weeks of my pregnancy and then I would move down to London to have my babies delivered by caesarean section at 37 weeks. This way, Professor Cohen could monitor both me and the babies during my pregnancy and delivery.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had discussed pregnancy in depth with Professor Cohen some 4 years earlier and the details of managing my blood condition alongside pregnancy and starting a family.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 23 January 2015, [Father of Babies A & B] and I attended at the Countess of Chester where I had my normal 12 week ultrasound, which confirmed I was pregnant with twins, and everything was normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 14 weeks I had a further scan at University College of London after suffering a small bleed. This was more of a reassurance scan. This scan again confirmed that everything was fine with both the babies and me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I continued to have regular scans at the Countess every 4 weeks and at 16 to 17 weeks I had a specialist scan again at the Countess of Chester Hospital with the consultant. This was to establish that there were no complications from the changeover in my medication from warfarin during the early stages of my pregnancy. This was because warfarin can cause abnormalities to an unborn baby if the change is delayed after the 6 week point. As my pregnancy was unplanned it was difficult to actually pinpoint the exact dates. The scan appeared normal and the babies were doing fine.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During my pregnancy I was under the care of two obstetricians at the Countess of Chester, Dr Davies and Dr Rowe. I continued with regular scans every 4 weeks and my blood pressure was monitored throughout my pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Everything was going fine until I reached 28 weeks.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I attended at my 28 week appointment where checks were carried out for diabetes. While I was at the appointment, I informed the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: midwife that I had started to suffer with what I can only describe as intense itching, especially in my hands and feet.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The scan was to check the babies were growing and everything was okay. After mentioning to the midwife the intense itching I was experiencing, she gave me a blood test and arranged an appointment with one of the consultants. While I was waiting for the consultant I was also given a leaflet relating to gestational cholestasis, which is a liver dysfunction and can cause stillborn babies during pregnancy. I was completely unaware of this at the time of telling the midwife, when I described this intense itching on my hands and feet.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember the appointment. It must have been a Saturday because [Father of Babies A & B] attended with me and we had made plans to go to the hospital for further tests and a scan and from there we intended to take a day trip to [Baby A] Bay in Anglesey. This is a place [Father of Babies A & B] and I have visited and we decided to name our son [Baby A] after.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When I returned to the hospital to speak to the consultant, further tests were carried out. My blood pressure was monitored and it was found to be on the high side. The nursing staff spoke to the on-call consultant who admitted me to hospital at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was admitted with pre-eclampsia due to the discovery of proteins in my urine. I remember being very upset as being admitted to hospital. I underwent several tests to try and diagnose what the problem was.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Davies, an obstetrician, suggested I was referred to a nephrologist [that's a kidney specialist] and a hepatologist [a liver specialist] as I had previously shown signs of protein in my urine before.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From all the tests carried out it was shown that my liver function was slightly off, so the doctors decided to start treatment for gestational cholestasis as a precaution along with blood pressure medication.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was extremely upset when the doctors informed me that I was going to be admitted to hospital. I was only a week away from going down to London under the care of Professor Cohen.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remained in hospital and I was closely monitored for approximately 3 weeks. My blood pressure had stabilised and I was providing urine samples daily to monitor the protein levels. Then, on 7 June 2015, around about 4 pm, I was just about to go to the cafeteria with my partner's mum, [redacted], and sister, [redacted], because it was outside the visiting times on the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: ward. The nursing staff asked to check my blood pressure before I left the ward to discover it was slightly raised. She carried on monitoring my blood pressure every 10 minutes to discover it was slowly rising every time it was taken.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember the nurse calling the on-call consultant, because I think it was Sunday and during the weekend the hospital have an on-call system between the consultants. The nurse provided the on-call consultant with my blood pressure readings and explained that it had continued to increase. I was immediately moved from the ward to the maternity labour suite in preparation for an emergency caesarean section. My blood pressure was taken every 5 minutes. I also had heart monitors attached to my abdomen to monitor the babies. A female doctor who delivered my babies (unfortunately, I can't recall her name) spoke to me and said she was going to speak to the anaesthetist to establish if I was going to have a spinal tap or be put to sleep under a general anaesthetic.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My blood pressure continued to rise and the doctors decided to carry out an emergency caesarean section.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was at this point now 31 weeks plus 2 days as an elective caesarean had been planned for the 32 week point.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember it was around 5 pm. I was taken into theatre, where I was given a general anaesthetic as it was too dangerous to wait for an epidural or spinal tap because my blood pressure was still rising and the medical staff were becoming concerned for the babies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was taken into theatre where an arterial line was placed into my arm to monitor my blood pressure internally.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My children were delivered at 8.30 pm. My baby girl was delivered weighing 3 pounds 11 ounces; we named her [Baby B]. One minute later, at 8.31 pm, my baby boy was delivered weighing 3 pounds 12 ounces. We named him [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Because my babies were delivered by caesarean section and I had been given a general anaesthetic, I was told I had to remain in bed, so I actually didn't get the opportunity to see my babies that night at all.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Father of Babies A & B] was in and out of the unit throughout the night and he took several photographs on the tablet of both [Baby A] and [Baby B] to show me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember a female doctor coming to me see the following morning; I think her name was Dr Rowe. She said she was surprised at how well I was doing, so I asked her if I could go
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: and see my babies. She said once I could get up and into a chair I'd be able to go and see them. At the time the doctors were trying to place long lines into both [Baby A] and [Baby B] and asked if I could wait a little while. I was getting a little anxious as I just wanted to see my children.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With the help of [Father of Babies A & B] and my mum, I managed to get washed and changed and into a wheelchair. It was probably around 12 to 1 pm on 8 June 2015. I hadn't seen my children and I was asking the staff to take me in to see them.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The registrar who was responsible for placing the long lines into [Baby B] and [Baby A] was a male doctor with a Scottish accent. His name was Andrew but I can't recall his surname. The only other member of staff I remember was a nurse with short hair by the name of Laura and when I was taken into the neonatal unit, she reminded me to wash my hands before touching my children. Both [Baby B] and [Baby A] were placed inside incubators. There was a small flap, or door, that allowed you to open and place your hand inside.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the time [Baby B] and [Baby A] remained in nursery 1. There was only one other cot in the same room, which was occupied by a baby boy."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And he, my Lord, has already been referred to as JE during the course of the opening:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He was born on 6 June 2015. Due to the amount of time I have spent in the neonatal department, I became very good friends with his mother.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When I first went into nursery 1, I immediately went straight over to [Baby B]. This was because she was the one who struggled with her breathing during delivery and needed medical assistance to start her breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby A] showed no signs of having any difficulties or problems. The only assistance [Baby A] had during the delivery was CPAP of just air.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There was a designated nurse checking and monitoring my babes. She was busy between the incubators of both [Baby A] and [Baby B]. I stayed with my twins for about an hour and I was told that I needed to get some rest myself but could come back later.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I returned back to the delivery room and I tried to rest following the advice of the nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Father of Babies A & B] and I had returned to the room to watch a little television and try to get some sleep. It was
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: around 8 pm. We had been in the room for about an hour and a half, watching a film, and I remember a male member of staff coming into the room. [Father of Babies A & B] heard him saying, 'you need to come quickly, there's something wrong with twin 2'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My mum and [Father of Babies A & B] helped me into the wheelchair and they quickly ran with me to the nursery where [Baby B] and [Baby A] were. All I can remember is being wheeled into this room, seeing what I can only describe felt like hundreds of people standing round [Baby A]'s incubator or cot and trying to resuscitate him. A nurse by the name of Caroline asked me if I was religious and if I would like her to say a prayer. A male doctor, Dr Jayaram, spoke to [Father of Babies A & B] and me and explained that the medical staff required our permission to stop CPR attempts on [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was so upset, I couldn't bring myself to say stop. I wanted them to carry on trying to help my baby.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was [Father of Babies A & B] who said to me, 'You have to, you're being cruel, you have to let him go, he's not there anymore'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Jayaram tried to say it me that if there was any possibility of ever getting him back at this stage he would have substantial physical and medical difficulties. With that, the only thing I could bring myself to do was nod my head, giving my permission to stop CPR attempts.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "One of the things that upsets me the most is I never had the opportunity to hold my son [Baby A] when he was alive. He remained in the incubator for the couple of hours I had to spend with him.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "One of the nurses, after [Baby A] died, asked if I would like to hold him; I don't remember who that nurse was. All of the medical equipment was removed from him, except for the tubing in his mouth, as we were told that had to remain in position for a post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby A] was placed in a hot cot while the arrangements for his transfer to Alder Hey Hospital for the post-mortem were made.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Father of Babies A & B] informed all the family. His mum and dad arrived at the hospital soon after they received the news. My mum was already with [Father of Babies A & B] and I at the hospital. My father lives approximately 2 hours away so it took him some time before he arrived.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After [Baby A] died I was frantic, anxious and extremely upset, and it was at that point I asked for somebody from the family to
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: remain with [Baby B] the whole time. I didn't want her out of my sight or to be left alone. My whole focus was on her then.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The next morning [Father of Babies A & B] and I moved to a room on the labour ward where we were given a private room for time to spend with [Baby A] before he was transferred to Alder Hey for a post-mortem. I can't remember the name of the nurse who looked after [Baby A], I was so upset.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She came into the labour room where [Father of Babies A & B] and I were waiting, she had [Baby A] wrapped up in her arms and she passed him to me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We sat quietly with him until the nurse returned and said that the transfer was ready. I didn't want to leave my little boy and I asked for extra time. The nurse gave us a few extra minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My mum and dad remained with [Baby B] while [Father of Babies A & B] and I said our goodbyes to our little boy. Once the transfer had been arranged and [Baby A] was taken off to Alder Hey, [Father of Babies A & B] and I returned back to the ward in nursery room 1 to be with [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we returned one of the nurses, again I can't recall her name, asked if I would like to hold [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She suggested that I went and changed into a loose-fitting top so [Baby B] could be placed onto my bare chest for body heat and skin-to-skin contact. The nurse told us that [Baby B] couldn't stay out of the incubator for long periods as her body temperature would drop and she needed to be kept warm.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I held [Baby B] close to my chest with feelings of joy and sadness at the same time. The nurse asked [Father of Babies A & B] if he wanted to hold his daughter. He was so scared because she was so tiny, he said no. [Baby B] happened to be very unsettled, she was crying a lot.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was around teatime, 5 to 6 pm. [Father of Babies A & B] and I hadn't had anything to eat and it was suggested that we went to get something. My mum and dad remained with [Baby B]. I had now been moved from the delivery labour ward into the Cestrian Ward at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Father of Babies A & B] and I returned back to the neonatal unit to see [Baby B] again, it was around 8 pm, when it was suggested by a member of the nursing staff that we went and got some rest. I can't remember exactly who from the nursing staff suggested leaving and getting rest.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Father of Babies A & B] and I did return to the room on the ward, we attempted to watch a film. I couldn't tell you what we tried to watch as I had fallen asleep. The next thing I knew [Father of Babies A & B] and I were getting woken by Lisa, a nurse from nursery room 4. She came into the room and I remember her saying, 'You need to come now'. My heart sank, not my baby, not again. [Father of Babies A & B] ran with me in the wheelchair into the neonatal unit and into nursery room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A female consultant on the neonatal unit was overseeing [Baby B]'s care. She explained to us both that [Baby B] had stabilised. It was a very similar situation to [Baby A]: [Baby B]'s heart and oxygen saturation levels had fallen rapidly.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The female consultant went on to describe seeing blotches/mottling across her skin, hand and feet. She asked our permission to take pictures/photographs of the mottling and she stated she had never seen this before.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remember being surprised that this was something she'd never witnessed before. I imagined a consultant of neonatal care would have seen everything. I cannot remember the consultant's name, but she is the only female consultant at the Countess of Chester neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Father of Babies A & B] and I had no problem with the staff photographing this mottling across [Baby B]'s chest, but by the time the staff had organised a camera it had disappeared. Both [Father of Babies A & B] and I stayed with [Baby B] all night. From that moment on I became frantic and terrified about leaving her. I always wanted a member of my family to be with her 24/7.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Looking back, prior to [Baby B]'s collapse during the day, she had been crying all the time. She was restless and wouldn't settle. It was if she was trying to tell me something was wrong. I wouldn't leave [Baby B]'s side.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was sleeping in a chair next to the cot incubator for a couple of days.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The following morning after [Baby B]'s collapse I did, however, take a photograph on my tablet of [Baby B]. She was back on a ventilator and stable, but I noticed that her hands and feet were still a little discoloured."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, [Mother of Babies A & B] exhibits the photograph as [redacted], which we're going to have on the screen now.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Photograph displayed to the court)
That, my Lord, was taken at 10.18 hours on 10 June, so later in the morning after events the night before:

"After a few days and nights sleeping in the chair next to [Baby B]'s cot one of the nurses suggested I would have to return back to the ward to sleep and went on to explain the hospital policy regarding the neonatal unit and the visiting hours. I reluctantly went back to the ward and after about a week I was discharged to go home.
"[Baby B] remained in hospital for a further 4 weeks.

She was actually in hospital a 4 weeks and 5 days before she came home. During that time [Baby B] remained on the neonatal unit. She was removed from nursery room 1 into nursery room 2. When [Baby B] was moved into nursery room 2, the nurse allocated to look after [Baby B] introduced herself to me. Again, I cannot recall her name.

"I do remember a brief conversation where she began talking to me as if I should know her. I remember apologising and saying, 'I'm really sorry, I don't remember you'. The nurse went on to explain that she was the nurse on duty the night [Baby A] died and she was the one who looked after him for us. She actually said, 'I looked after [Baby A] for you the night he died'.
"The only names I can recall of nurses working from nursery 1 in the neonatal unit when [Baby A] and [Baby B] were admitted were nurses [Nurse A], Caroline and Laura.
Nursery nurse Nicky and nurses Lisa and Liz also worked on the neonatal unit, but I think they worked for different nursery rooms, I'm not sure.

"Once I was discharged from hospital, I would get up in the morning and head straight for the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. I was always there at 9 am. Occasionally, I would arrive no later than 9.30 am, and I would stay with [Baby B] all day. [Father of Babies A & B] and I would leave the neonatal unit once the night shift staff had come on duty and we knew who was looking after [Baby B] throughout the night. I would always say to the nurse dealing with her to update us, no matter what.

"Because of what happened with [Baby A] and [Baby B] having a collapse also, I was and still am extremely protective of her. So throughout [Baby B]'s time in the hospital when I wasn't there, which is only during the night-time, every 2 hours either [Father of Babies A & B] or I would call the parent telephone number and ask how things were with [Baby B]. We would ask to speak to the designated nurse who was looking after [Baby B]

that evening and ask for an update. I would set an alarm on my mobile phone every 2 hours throughout the night and call. On occasions I do recall some of the nurses telling me to get some rest as everything was fine and they would tell me that they would call if needed, but I couldn't help it: I needed to call.

"I remember one night -- it was around 4 am I think -- I had called the designated parent line and a female voice answered it. I would have said who I was, [Baby B]'s mother, I presume the female voice was one of the nursing staff on the unit, I remember her saying, 'Just wait a moment'. The next voice I heard was a male voice, I recognised it as Dr Andrew -- I don't know his surname but he has a distinctive Scottish accent. He said, 'I have given', and then a name which I can't remember but it certainly wasn't [Baby B], 'something number of CC of adrenaline, are you coming in?' I remember in a daze replying back to him, 'Do you think I need to come in? I'm phoning about [Baby B], it's [Baby B]'s mum'. I could hear the panic and change in tone in his voice as if he had disclosed something to me which had nothing to do with [Baby B]. I was then put through to the nurse dealing with [Baby B] that night and was informed she was fast asleep and doing well, nothing to worry about.
I remember saying to her, 'If there is anything please let us know'. The nurse reassured me everything was okay and I hung up.

"At the Countess of Chester Hospital unit they have a designated telephone line or number that they provide to parents to allow them direct access to the unit to speak with the nursing staff and get an update on how their baby is doing. I used to have the telephone number stored in my mobile phone but I have unfortunately deleted it.

"Following [Baby A]'s death, [Father of Babies A & B] and I have searched for a reason as to why. It was suggested by one consultant at the hospital that if the finding from [Baby A]'s post-mortem came back inconclusive, it may well have something to do with my blood condition [that being the APS that we discussed]. I was furious when this was suggested and, following [Baby B]'s discharge from hospital, [Father of Babies A & B] and I asked for some answers, which we never really got. We did receive a letter from one of the consultants who attempted to answer some of our concerns."
My Lord, that concludes the statement from [Mother of Babies A & B].
Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of [Father of Babies A & B] (read)
The next statement to read, ladies and gentlemen, is that of [Father of Babies A & B]. Having signed the declaration which is dated on this occasion 27 September 2019, he says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am [Father of Babies A & B] but everybody calls me by my middle name [Father of Babies A & B]. [Mother of Babies A & B] and I met approximately 7 years ago through a mutual friend and we have been together ever since. I was aware right from the beginning of our relationship that [Mother of Babies A & B] had been diagnosed with a rare blood disorder called APS.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During the winter of 2014, following an extended four-month holiday visiting family in Australia, [Mother of Babies A & B] and I returned home to the UK to discover that [Mother of Babies A & B] had fallen pregnant. It was on 13 December 2014, the day before my 30th birthday, that we discovered [Mother of Babies A & B] was pregnant. This wasn't a planned pregnancy and our initial thoughts were around [Mother of Babies A & B]' diagnosis and her use of warfarin. I remember [Mother of Babies A & B] visiting her GP at first and was immediately switched medication to a safer option during pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From that initial meeting with the GP, arrangements were made for [Mother of Babies A & B] and I to travel to London to see [Mother of Babies A & B]'s specialist, Professor Cohen, who was already looking after [Mother of Babies A & B]. An appointment was made with Professor Cohen, and [Mother of Babies A & B] and I travelled down the following week to discuss the pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Professor Cohen discussed with us at length how to manage [Mother of Babies A & B]'s pregnancy. The decision was made that Professor Cohen would manage her blood condition [that's the APS], working alongside the Countess of Chester Hospital, who would look after the antenatal care.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was going to remain at home up to 30 weeks of her pregnancy and then she was going to move down to London to have our babies delivered by caesarean section at 37 weeks. That way, Professor Cohen could monitor both [Mother of Babies A & B] and our babies during her pregnancy and delivery.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 23 January 2015 [Mother of Babies A & B] and I attended at the Countess of Chester where [Mother of Babies A & B] had her 12 week ultrasound, which confirmed that she was pregnant with twins and everything was fine and normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Around the 14-week point [Mother of Babies A & B] suffered a small bleed. Arrangements had been made for a further scan at University College of London with Dr Cohen, and this was more of
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: a reassurance scan. This scan again confirmed that everything was fine with both the babies and [Mother of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] continued to have regular scans at the Countess every 4 weeks and at 16-17 weeks she had a specialist scan, again at the Countess of Chester, with the consultant. This was to establish that there were no complications from the changeover in her medication, from the warfarin, during the early stages of her pregnancy when she was unaware that she was pregnant.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] knew of the complications warfarin may cause during the early part of any pregnancy. It was explained to us that warfarin can cause abnormalities to an unborn baby if the change in medication for APS is delayed after the 6-week point. As our pregnancy was unplanned, it was difficult to actually pinpoint the exact date and this scan was hopefully going to assist with that. The scan appeared normal and the babies were doing fine. This was very reassuring to both [Mother of Babies A & B] and I.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During [Mother of Babies A & B]'s pregnancy she was monitored carefully. She was under the care of two obstetricians at the Countess of Chester Hospital, Dr Davies and Dr Rowe, and she continued to have regular scans every 4 weeks and her blood pressure was monitored throughout her pregnancy. Everything was going fine until she reached 28-week point when [Mother of Babies A & B] started getting these intense itching sensations in her hands and feet.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Mother of Babies A & B] had an appointment arranged at 28 weeks. One of the checks carried out was for diabetes and while we were at this appointment [Mother of Babies A & B] informed the midwife that she had started suffering from what she described as intense itching, especially in her hands and feet.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The scan was to check that the babies were growing and everything was okay. After mentioning to the midwife the intense itching that [Mother of Babies A & B] was experiencing, the midwife gave [Mother of Babies A & B] a blood test and arranged an appointment with one of the consultants.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: While we were waiting for the consultant, [Mother of Babies A & B] was given a leaflet relating to gestational cholestasis, describing a liver dysfunction that can cause stillborn babies during pregnancy. One of the symptoms is itching to skin. Both [Mother of Babies A & B] and I were completely unaware of this at the time of telling the midwife.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The appointment must have been on a Saturday because I remember going with [Mother of Babies A & B] to the appointment.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We planned to go to the hospital for the tests and the scan and from there we intended on taking a day trip to [Baby A] Bay in Anglesey. This is a place we had visited and also decided to name our son [Baby A] after.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we returned to the hospital to speak to the consultant further tests were carried out, [Mother of Babies A & B]'s blood pressure was monitored, and it was found to be on the high side. The nursing staff spoke to the on-call consultant who admitted [Mother of Babies A & B] to hospital at the Countess of Chester Hospital. [Mother of Babies A & B] was immediately admitted on to a ward with pre-eclampsia due to the discovery of proteins in her urine.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] underwent several tests to try and diagnose what the problem was. Dr Davies, an obstetrician, suggested she was referred to a nephrologist, a kidney specialist, and hepatologist, a liver specialist, as she had previously shown signs of protein in her urine.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: From all the tests carried out it was shown that her liver function was slightly off so the doctors decided to start treatment for gestational cholestasis as a precaution, along with blood pressure medication.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was extremely upset when the doctors informed her that she was going to be admitted to hospital. She was only a week away from going to London under the care of Professor Cohen. [Mother of Babies A & B] contacted Dr Cohen directly to see if it was still possible to be transferred to London but it was just too risky for both [Mother of Babies A & B] and the babies, so [Mother of Babies A & B] remained in hospital and was closely monitored for approximately 2 weeks. Her blood pressure had stabilised."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And it said she was monitored closely:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 7 June 2015, around 4 pm, my mother, [redacted], and my sister visited the hospital. It was outside the visiting time, so [Mother of Babies A & B] and I had arranged to meet them in the café. The nursing staff asked to check [Mother of Babies A & B]'s blood pressure before we left the ward, only to discover it was slightly raised.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The nursing staff wouldn't let [Mother of Babies A & B] off the ward they carried on monitoring her blood pressure every 10 minutes only to discover it was slowly rising every time it was taken. One of the medical staff asked for a consultant to be called, but because it was the weekend the hospital have an oncall system between the consultants. This took some time and
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: when the consultant arrived, the nurse gave the on-call consultant [Mother of Babies A & B]'s blood pressure readings and explained that it had continued to increase.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At that point [Mother of Babies A & B] was immediately moved from the ward to the maternity labour suite in preparation for an emergency caesarean section. Her blood pressure was taken every 5 minutes. She also had heart monitors attached to her abdomen to monitor the babies too.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The female doctor who delivered our babies -- again unfortunately I can't recall her name [says the statement] -spoke to [Mother of Babies A & B] and I and explained that she was going to speak with the anaesthetist to establish if [Mother of Babies A & B] was going to have a spinal tap or be put to sleep under general anaesthetic.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B]'s blood pressure continued to rise and the doctors decided to carry out an emergency caesarean section. [Mother of Babies A & B] was now 31 weeks plus 2 days and an elective caesarean had been planned for the 32-week point.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was taken into theatre around 5 pm. She was given a general anaesthetic. It was explained to us that it was too dangerous to wait for an epidural or spinal tap, because of [Mother of Babies A & B]'s rising blood pressure, and the medical staff were becoming concerned for the babies. I remained just outside the surgical theatre with [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum, waiting for some news."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)

You probably knew, but just for the avoidance of doubt, spinal tap is not a spinal anaesthetic. It's not the same as an epidural. That used to be an epidural, but now it's a spinal anaesthetic though. But it's not relevant here because she had a general anaesthetic, as you heard.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's in the alternative in the statement but as my Lord rightly pointed out --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's already been put in evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "I was standing in the corridor [says [Father of Babies A & B]] with [Grandmother of Babies A & B] when a nurse came out of theatre pushing a cot. She briefly stopped for moments to introduce me to my son, [Baby A], and then carried straight on into the neonatal unit. [Baby B] was still in the theatre room.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Our children were delivered at 8.30 pm. Our baby girl was delivered weighing 3 pounds 11 ounces and we named her [Baby B]. One minute later, at 8.31 pm, our baby boy was delivered weighing 3 pounds 12 ounces, we named him [Baby A]. Because our babies were delivered by emergency caesarean section, [Mother of Babies A & B] had to be given a general anaesthetic, so following the operation she had to remain in bed and rest, so she did not actually get the opportunity to see our children until the following day. I was in and out of the neonatal unit throughout the night and took several photographs on the tablet of both [Baby A] and [Baby B] to show [Mother of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] had told the family that no one is to go in and see our children before she is able to, except me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I accessed the neonatal unit via the door at just across from the theatre entrance."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord will remember we looked at just that doorway between theatre and the neonatal and just how close it is on the plan this morning:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I would ring the bell where Lucy, a member of the nursing staff, would open the door every time I went through.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Following [Mother of Babies A & B]'s surgery, we Skyped members of our family, including her brother and sister. [Mother of Babies A & B] contacted her father, who lives in Lincolnshire, to let him know everybody was doing well. I remained with [Mother of Babies A & B] throughout the night in the labour room and the following morning, Dr Rowe, [Mother of Babies A & B]'s obstetrician, visited. [Mother of Babies A & B] kept asking to go and see the babies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Rowe said, 'Once you are able to get up and get into a wheelchair, then you'll be able to go and see your babies'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the time the doctors in the neonatal ward were trying to place long lines into both [Baby A] and [Baby B] and asked if we could wait a little while. [Mother of Babies A & B] was getting very anxious; she just wanted to see our children.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was probably around 12 to 1 pm on 8 June 2015 when [Mother of Babies A & B] got to see the babies for the first time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: With the help of [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum we managed to get [Mother of Babies A & B] washed and changed and into a wheelchair; I think one of the difficulties was [Mother of Babies A & B] still had a drip in her arm.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The registrar who was responsible for placing the long lines into [Baby A] and [Baby B] was a male doctor with a Scottish accent. [Mother of Babies A & B] thinks his name was Andrew but she can't recall the surname.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When the babies go into the neonatal unit there is a nurse who is designated to look after them during their shift. A nurse I called Lucy was looking after [Baby B] and [Baby A]. I remember her because I was nervous about the machines and she went through and explained what each of them was to make me feel better.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby B] and [Baby A] were taken straight from the theatre into nursery room 1 on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I believe there was one other cot which was occupied by another baby in nursery room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We helped [Mother of Babies A & B] into a wheelchair and took her from the labour ward into the neonatal unit to see the twins. This was the first time [Mother of Babies A & B] had seen the twins. We went into nursery room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] went straight over to [Baby B]. This was simply because [Baby B] was the baby we were informed had struggled to start breathing during delivery and needed medical assistance to start her breathing off. [Baby A] was breathing for himself, with the added help of CPAP additional air. [Baby A] wasn't ventilated. I remember seeing [Baby B] first as [Baby A] started to cry when he heard [Mother of Babies A & B] talking.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On this occasion we stayed on the unit for about an hour. The nursing staff were busy between the two incubators of both [Baby A] and [Baby B]. [Mother of Babies A & B] hadn't slept very much at this point and it was suggested that she should she get some rest and come back later.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I tried to persuade [Mother of Babies A & B] to get some rest and we returned back to the delivery room to rest following the advice of the staff. Myself and [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum sat with [Mother of Babies A & B] while she had a rest.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had been in the room for about an hour and a half when myself and her mum heard a commotion outside the room and a nurse called [Nurse A] said, 'There's something wrong with twin 2". [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum and I both looked at each other, worried, and after a few minutes a male member of staff came into the room and said, 'You need to come quick, it's twin 2'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Along with the help of [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum, we got [Mother of Babies A & B] into a wheelchair and quickly ran down to the nursery 1 where [Baby B] and [Baby A] were. All I can remember is wheeling [Mother of Babies A & B] into the room and seeing what I can only describe as hundreds of people standing around [Baby A]'s incubator/cot trying to resuscitate him. [Mother of Babies A & B] became extremely upset. I remember a nurse called Caroline asking us if we were religious and if we would like her to say a prayer.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Jayaram, one of the consultants, spoke to Loise and I and explained that the medical staff had tried all they could, and it's now been some time, and there have been no improvements. He went on to say they needed our permission to stop CPR attempts on [Baby A]. We were both so upset neither one of us could bring ourselves to say stop. We just wanted them to carry on trying to save our baby boy. [Mother of Babies A & B] was hysterical. After I'd gathered my thoughts I said to [Mother of Babies A & B] something along the lines of, 'We have to let him go, he's not there anymore, we have to let him go'. It's one of the most difficult things I've ever had to do, to let my son go.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The consultant, Dr Jayaram, spoke to [Mother of Babies A & B] and I and informed us that if there was any possibility of ever getting him back at this stage, it's likely he would have substantial physical and medical difficulties in the future. With that, the only kind thing I could bring myself to do was to tell [Mother of Babies A & B] to let him go.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She nodded her head towards Dr Jayaram, giving our permission to stop CPR attempts. One thing that upsets [Mother of Babies A & B] and I the most is we never had the opportunity to hold our son [Baby A] when he was alive. We were told he was doing fine, he was breathing for himself and doing well.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby A] was then moved into a hot cot and it was put next to [Baby B]. We remained in nursery room 1 with [Baby B] and I tried to comfort [Mother of Babies A & B]. The room seemed to empty quickly, leaving only a couple of nurses to assist [Mother of Babies A & B] and I. I can only presume the staff were trying to give us some privacy. The doctor and the consultant stayed to write up their notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "One of the nurses asked if we would like to hold [Baby A]. I don't remember who that nurse was, but [Mother of Babies A & B] immediately said that she did. All of the medical equipment was removed from [Baby A] except for the tubing in his mouth. We were told that had to remain in position for the post-mortem. We understood the reason for that. [Baby A] was placed into a cot directly next to [Baby B]'s incubator and arrangements were then
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: made for [Baby A] to be transferred to Alder Hey Hospital for the post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember asking [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum if she could start informing all the family. My mum and dad arrived at the hospital soon after they received the news. [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum was already with us at the hospital. Her father lives about 2 hours away, so it took him some time before he arrived.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After [Baby A] died we were both pretty anxious and upset and it was at this point [Mother of Babies A & B] wouldn't leave [Baby B]'s side unless a member of the family was there the whole time. She just didn't want [Baby B] to be out of my sight or to be left alone. [Mother of Babies A & B]'s whole focus was on [Baby B], but [Mother of Babies A & B] was still recovering from surgery herself and I tried to get [Mother of Babies A & B] to go back and rest a little back in the room while I remained with [Baby B] and [Baby A] on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was sat with my father next to [Baby B] in nursery room 1 most of the night while [Mother of Babies A & B] rested and during this time [Mother of Babies A & B]'s father arrived at the hospital. He sat with [Mother of Babies A & B] for about an hour or more trying to comfort her and then he came in to see [Baby B] and [Baby A] together.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The next morning [Mother of Babies A & B] and I were on the labour ward where we were given a private room to spend time with [Baby A] before he was transferred to Alder Hey Hospital for post-mortem. [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum and dad remained with [Baby B] on the neonatal unit while we said our goodbyes. I remember the name of the nurse -- it was Lucy -- that brought [Baby A] in to us as we were both so upset. She came into the labour room where [Mother of Babies A & B] and I were waiting. She had [Baby A] in his hot cot and she passed him over to [Mother of Babies A & B]. We sat quietly with him until Lucy returned and said the transfer was ready. We just didn't want to leave our baby boy and [Mother of Babies A & B] asked for a few minutes. The nurse left the room and gave us those few extra minutes to say our final goodbye.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I know a memory box was done for [Baby A] but I don't know who did it or when it was done.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we returned back to the neonatal unit, one of the nurses called Jo asked if we would like to hold [Baby B]. She was so small I didn't want to hurt her so I said no but [Mother of Babies A & B] said she would like to hold [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The nurse, Jo, suggested that [Mother of Babies A & B] went and got changed into a loose-fitting top so [Baby B] could be placed
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: on to [Mother of Babies A & B]'s bare chest for body heat and skin-to-skin contact. This helps with heat and the baby can hear your heartbeat also.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The nurse Jo told us that [Baby B] couldn't stay out of the incubator for long periods as her body temperature would drop and she needed to be kept warm.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Mother of Babies A & B] held [Baby B] close to her chest. It was lovely to see, but there were feelings of both joy and sadness.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was around teatime, between 5 and 6 pm on 9 June 2015, both [Mother of Babies A & B] and I hadn't had anything to eat and it was suggested we went to get something.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Mother of Babies A & B]'s parents remained with [Baby B], and [Mother of Babies A & B] had now been moved from the delivery labour room on to the Cestrian Ward at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At about 8 pm, [Mother of Babies A & B] and I returned back to the neonatal unit to see [Baby B] again. It was shortly after the shift changeover and the night staff had come on duty. The designated nurse had introduced herself; again, I can't remember names. It was suggested by [Mother of Babies A & B]'s mum and dad, as well as all the nursing staff, that we went and got some rest. [Mother of Babies A & B] and I had at this point had had very little sleep. All of the family had gone home to get some sleep and I suggested to [Mother of Babies A & B] that we needed to do the same. This was the first time [Baby B] was going to be left without a member of family since [Baby A] had passed away.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We did return to the room on the ward. We attempted to watch a film -- I couldn't tell you what we tried to watch as I think we had both fallen asleep very quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next thing we knew, we were getting woken by a nursery nurse, her name was Lisa. She came into the room and said something along the lines of, 'You need to come now'. I didn't know what to think. My heart sank.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I ran with [Mother of Babies A & B] in the wheelchair into the neonatal unit and into nursery room 1. The female consultant on the neonatal unit was overseeing [Baby B]'s care. She explained to us both that [Baby B] had now stabilised, she had experienced a very similar situation to [Baby A], and [Baby B]'s heart and oxygen saturation levels had fallen rapidly. The female consultant went on to describe seeing blotches or mottling across her skin and feet. She asked our permission to take pictures of the mottling as she said she had never seen this before. I remember being surprised that this was something she
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: had never witnessed before with her experience. You imagine a consultant in neonatal care would have seen almost everything.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I can't remember the consultant's name. I also remember her looking at the nurse as she left and crossing her fingers and saying, 'Good luck', as in hoping [Baby B] would be okay.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had no problem with the staff photographing this mottling across [Baby B]'s chest. By the time the staff had organised a camera it had disappeared. [Mother of Babies A & B] was given a comfy recliner chair and slept by [Baby B]'s incubator all night. [Mother of Babies A & B] asked the staff if they could make her leave and they said no, so she stayed.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Both [Mother of Babies A & B] and I remained with [Baby B] all night. From that moment on [Mother of Babies A & B] became frantic about leaving her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The following morning after [Baby B]'s collapse we both noticed that her hands and feet were still a little discoloured. [Mother of Babies A & B] took a photograph on her tablet and at this point [Baby B] was back on a ventilator and stable."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that's the photograph we looked at earlier.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Two days after [Baby B] collapsed, her colour was back to normal, apart from a small mark across her chest. At this point one of the nurses suggested we would have to return back to the ward to sleep and went on to explain the hospital policy regarding the neonatal unit and visiting hours. [Mother of Babies A & B] reluctantly went back to the ward and, after about a week, she was discharged to go home. However during [Mother of Babies A & B]'s time in hospital and after she is discharged, she would arrive on the neonatal unit first thing in the morning and wouldn't leave until the day staff had changed so she knew who was looking after [Baby B] overnight.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby B] remained in hospital for a further 4 weeks.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was hospital in hospital a total of 4 weeks and 5 days before she came home. During that time [Baby B] remained on the neonatal unit. She was removed from nursery 1 through to nursery 4. At this point I had returned back to work and [Mother of Babies A & B] was still going to the hospital on a daily basis.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Once [Mother of Babies A & B] was discharged from hospital she would get up in the morning and head straight to the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. She would be there around 9 am and would stay with [Baby B] all day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would go straight to the hospital after work and [Mother of Babies A & B] and I would leave the neonatal unit once the night shift staff had come on duty and we knew who it was looking after [Baby B] throughout the night. [Mother of Babies A & B] would ask the designated nurse who was looking after [Baby B] that if anything should happen we wanted to be updated, no matter what.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Because of what happened with [Baby A] and [Baby B] suffering a collapse, we both became and still are extremely protective of our daughter, so throughout [Baby B]'s time in hospital when we weren't there, which was only during the night-time, every 2 hours either I or [Mother of Babies A & B] would call the parent telephone number and ask how things were with [Baby B]. We would ask to speak to the designated nurse was looking after [Baby B] for that shift and ask for an update. We even set an alarm on one of our mobile phones every 2 hours throughout the night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember one occasion one evening, it was probably around 4 am, [Mother of Babies A & B] had called the designated parent line to see how [Baby B] was doing. She was mistakenly put through to one of the doctors. When she came off the phone [Mother of Babies A & B] told me that the doctor must have thought he was speaking to someone different.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I believe [Mother of Babies A & B] was then put through to the designated nurse dealing with [Baby B] that night and was informed she was fast asleep and doing well and nothing to worry about, everything was okay.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the Countess of Chester neonatal unit they have a designated telephone line number they provide to allow direct access to the unit for parents to speak to the nursing staff and get an update on how their baby is doing. Both [Mother of Babies A & B] and I would have had this number stored in our mobile phones but have unfortunately deleted it now."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes the statement of [Father of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of [Grandmother of Babies A & B] (read)
At this stage finally to be read is the statement of [Grandmother of Babies A & B]. Same declaration, on this occasion dated 17 April 2019. And [Grandmother of Babies A & B] says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am the mother to [Mother of Babies A & B] and grandmother to [Baby A] and [Baby B]. In September 2017, [Mother of Babies A & B] and [Father of Babies A & B] received the news they had been waiting for: they had been accepted and began making all the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: necessary arrangements by December 2017 to move to start their new life in Australia. [Father of Babies A & B]'s full name is [Father of Babies A & B]; everybody calls him by his middle name [Father of Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During the winter of 2014, following an extended holiday to Australia visiting family, [Mother of Babies A & B] and [Father of Babies A & B] returned home to the UK only to discover [Mother of Babies A & B] was pregnant and expecting twins. This came as a big surprise to everyone as it wasn't a planned pregnancy, but we were all thrilled.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When [Mother of Babies A & B] and [Father of Babies A & B] returned home from their holiday in Australia and discovered that [Mother of Babies A & B] was pregnant our initial thoughts were around [Mother of Babies A & B]'s diagnosis of APS and what to do next. [Mother of Babies A & B] was closely monitored throughout her pregnancy and attended all of her appointments, some of which took place in London with Professor Cohen, the specialist.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was agreed at 30 weeks [Mother of Babies A & B] and I would move down to London where Professor Cohen would closely monitor [Mother of Babies A & B]'s condition and advise the antenatal team of [Mother of Babies A & B]'s condition during delivery of the twins.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Around 28/29 weeks, [Mother of Babies A & B] went for a routine check-up with the midwife at the Countess of Chester Hospital. At that point, [Mother of Babies A & B] had started to suffer with intense itching to her hands and feet. Unbeknown to us, this was a side effect of gestational colitis (sic), which affects the liver. [Mother of Babies A & B] was given blood tests and referred to one of the consultants. When she returned to the hospital to speak to the consultant, further blood tests were carried out and her blood pressure was monitored, which was found to be on the high side. The advice was then to admit [Mother of Babies A & B] to hospital to monitor both her and the babies closely. It was approaching a bank holiday weekend when [Mother of Babies A & B] was taken into hospital. She was placed on to antenatal ward and monitored.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was fine and during her time in hospital the two of us would go for little walks around the grounds, visiting the cafeteria for a sandwich and a cup of tea.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Then, on Sunday, 7 June 2015 -- it must have been early afternoon -- [Mother of Babies A & B]'s blood pressure began to rise. The doctors and nursing staff monitored [Mother of Babies A & B] throughout the afternoon. I remained with [Mother of
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Babies A & B] and [Father of Babies A & B] at the hospital until about 4 pm in the afternoon when I decided to return home.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A couple of hours later I received a phone call from [Father of Babies A & B]; it was probably around 6 pm. He informed me that [Mother of Babies A & B]'s blood pressure wasn't coming down and the doctors were concerned for the babies. A decision had been made to take [Mother of Babies A & B] into theatre for an emergency caesarean section and can I make it back to the hospital. When I arrived back at the hospital [Mother of Babies A & B] had been moved into the labour ward and was placed into one of the delivery rooms. I think she was the second room in from the double doors leading into the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The staff were monitoring [Mother of Babies A & B] constantly and preparing her for theatre. [Father of Babies A & B] and I were both very anxious at this point as the medical staff wheeled [Mother of Babies A & B] into the theatre room. [Father of Babies A & B] and I remained outside the theatre for approximately an hour. It felt like a lifetime.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After an anxious wait in the corridor, the doors to the theatre opened and we briefly saw one of the nurses whizzing past with an incubator, straight into the special care unit. It was [Baby A] getting transferred.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that moment I could hear what I would describe as a commotion in the theatre. I was unable to see what was happening. My initial reaction was, is everything okay with [Mother of Babies A & B], and after several minutes a second incubator went flying past us in the corridor and went straight into the neonatal special care unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was [Baby B] getting transferred from the theatre on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Moments later, a female doctor came out to see [Father of Babies A & B] and me. She explained although [Baby A] was transferred first on to the special unit, it was [Baby B] who was born at 8.30 pm, followed a minute later by [Baby A] at 8.31.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies A & B] was quite poorly after the caesarean section and was taken back to the labour ward to recover. She was unable to go and see her children that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think I remember [Father of Babies A & B] going to see the babies and took several photographs to show [Mother of Babies A & B] but I can't be certain if it was that night or the following morning.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Father of Babies A & B] and I both remained with [Mother of Babies A & B] that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I do remember [Mother of Babies A & B] telling the whole family that nobody is allowed to see the babies until she and [Father of Babies A & B] had seen them first.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Because [Mother of Babies A & B] was so poorly and unable to get into a wheelchair following the caesarean section, the nursing staff from the special care unit came in to update [Mother of Babies A & B], reassuring her and [Father of Babies A & B] that the babies were doing well and both fine.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The evening the babies were delivered, Sunday, 7 June 2015, I remained at the hospital with [Father of Babies A & B] and [Mother of Babies A & B]. At some point the following day I went home for a couple of hours. It was had when I returned back to the hospital I called in to see the babies for the first time. They were both together in nursery room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby B]'s incubator was lengthways on the right-hand side with, the bottom of the incubator as you entered the room. [Baby A] was directly in front of you as you entered in nursery 1. I am not sure if there was one or two other babies in the room but I do remember another little baby boy; he was on the left-hand side of nursery room 1. [Father of Babies A & B] and [Mother of Babies A & B] got to know his parents and remained friendly after the children left the hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I only popped in to see the babies for a very brief moment before returning back to the labour ward as I was so worried about [Mother of Babies A & B]. [Baby A] was breathing for himself and on CPAP (he wasn't intubated), he was a lovely pink colour with his little arms and legs moving. Both [Baby A] and [Baby B] appeared very small and fragile to me. [Baby B] was intubated at the time and not moving as much as [Baby A]. I only stayed in nursery room 1 a few moments before returning back to [Mother of Babies A & B] on the labour ward.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Throughout the day [Mother of Babies A & B] was asking the staff if she could go and visit the babies. At one point she was informed that the doctors were trying to get long lines into the twins to assist with their nutrition and was asked to wait a little while.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At some point during the afternoon [Mother of Babies A & B], [Father of Babies A & B] and I were told we could go and see the babies. It was no easy task as we had to get [Mother of Babies A & B] up out of bed and into a wheelchair. At the time she was still on a drip after the operation. I am not sure of the time, it may have been around 3 or 4 pm. I can't remember the names of
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: the nursing staff or who was there at the time. I don't think we stayed very long with the babies at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The midwives were concerned and insisted that [Mother of Babies A & B] return back to the labour room to rest and recover from the caesarean section.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was Monday evening, 8 June 2015, about 8.30 to 9 pm, again I can't be certain of the exact time.
